t: In motor third party law, a 'tortfeasor' is best described as:
o: The person who suffers loss because of another's wrongful act
The insurer who indemnifies the owner against liability
The person who commits the wrongful act causing loss to another
The Tribunal that adjudicates the compensation claim
e: A tortfeasor is the wrongdoer. When held legally liable, the tortfeasor (or those vicariously liable for him) must compensate the injured party for the damage caused.

t: Under Section 145 of the MV Act as amended in 2019, the expression 'third party' expressly includes:
o: The owner of the insured vehicle and his family members
Gratuitous passengers in a goods carriage
The Government, the driver and any other co-worker on a transport vehicle
The Government only
e: Section 145(i) as amended includes the Government, the driver and any other co-worker on a transport vehicle within 'third party'. Earlier the definition included only the Government.

t: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 consists of:
o: 11 Chapters, 145 Sections and 1 Schedule
14 Chapters, 217 Sections and 2 Schedules
12 Chapters, 176 Sections and 2 Schedules
14 Chapters, 217 Sections and 1 Schedule
e: The MV Act 1988 has 14 Chapters, 217 Sections and one Schedule. Third party insurance and Claims Tribunals are dealt with in Chapters XI and XII (Sections 145 to 176).

t: The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 was notified on 09.08.2019 and its main provisions came into force from:
e: The Amendment Act was notified on 9 August 2019 and implemented from 1 September 2019; the rules on investigation and settlement of claims (the detailed accident report scheme) came into effect from 1 April 2022.

t: Under Section 164 of the amended MV Act, the fixed no-fault compensation payable for grievous hurt is:
e: Section 164 fixes ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt, payable without proof of negligence. Nothing is payable under s.164 for minor injury.

t: The compensation for death in a hit-and-run motor accident under the amended Section 161 is:
e: The 2019 amendment raised hit-and-run compensation from ₹25,000 to ₹2,00,000 for death and from ₹12,500 to ₹50,000 for grievous hurt.

t: Under Section 164, the fixed compensation payable in the case of death is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 164 provides ₹5 lakh for death and ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt, payable by the owner or insurer without proof of wrongful act or neglect.

t: Which Chapter of the MV Act, dealing with 'Liability without fault in certain cases' (Sections 140–144), was deleted by the 2019 amendment?
o: Chapter XII
Chapter IX
Chapter X
Chapter XI
e: Chapter X (Sections 140–144) on no-fault interim liability was omitted; no-fault compensation is now a fixed, final payment under the new Section 164 in Chapter XI.

t: After the 2019 amendment, an application for compensation under Section 166 must be made within:
o: Six months of the occurrence of the accident
Ninety days of the occurrence of the accident
Twelve months of the occurrence of the accident
Two years of the occurrence of the accident
e: The amended s.166(3) reintroduced a limitation of six months from the accident; under the pre-amendment law there was no time limit for filing a claim petition.

t: An appeal against an award of the Claims Tribunal lies to the High Court within:
o: 90 days from the date of the award
180 days from the date of the award
30 days from the date of the award
60 days from the date of the award
e: Section 173 allows any aggrieved person to appeal to the High Court within ninety days of the award, subject to the deposit condition and the one-lakh threshold.

t: Under Section 169, for the purpose of adjudicating claims the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal:
o: Has all the powers of a Civil Court and is deemed to be a Civil Court
Has the powers of a Magistrate of the first class
Is bound by the strict rules of the Code of Civil Procedure
Has the powers of a Labour Court under the Industrial Disputes Act
e: Section 169 confers on the Claims Tribunal all the powers of a Civil Court and deems it a Civil Court for all purposes, while allowing a summary procedure.

t: Interest awarded by a Claims Tribunal under Section 171 of the MV Act is:
o: Simple interest from a date not earlier than the date of making the claim
Simple interest from the date of the accident only
Interest at the bank rate from the date of the award only
Compound interest from the date of the accident
e: Section 171 provides for simple interest at such rate and from such date, not earlier than the date of making the claim, as the Tribunal specifies.

t: Causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, formerly Section 304A IPC, is now punishable under which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
o: Section 125
Section 101
Section 106
Section 281
e: Section 304A IPC corresponds to Section 106 BNS. Section 281 BNS is rash driving (old 279 IPC) and Section 125 BNS covers acts endangering life (old 337/338 IPC).

t: In Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) the Supreme Court held that a claimant in a death case must establish three facts. These are:
o: Age, educational qualification and marital status of the deceased
Income, place of residence and nature of employment of the deceased
Negligence of the driver, speed of the vehicle and the injuries sustained
Age, income and number of dependants of the deceased
e: Sarla Verma standardised the computation: age of the deceased (for the multiplier), income (for the multiplicand) and the number of dependants (for the personal-expense deduction).

t: As per the multiplier table approved in Pranay Sethi, the multiplier applicable where the deceased was aged 41 to 45 years is:
e: The Sarla Verma table starts at 18 for ages 15–25 and reduces by one per five-year band: 17 (26–30), 16 (31–35), 15 (36–40), 14 (41–45), 13 (46–50), then 11, 9, 7 and 5.

t: Under Pranay Sethi, for a deceased below 40 years holding a permanent job, the addition for future prospects is:
o: 25% of actual salary
40% of actual salary
30% of actual salary
50% of actual salary
e: Salaried persons on a permanent job get 50% (below 40), 30% (40–50) and 15% (above 50). Self-employed or fixed-salary persons get 40%, 25% and 10% respectively.

t: The amounts fixed by Pranay Sethi (2017) under the conventional heads of loss of estate, loss of consortium and funeral expenses were respectively:
e: Pranay Sethi fixed loss of estate ₹15,000, loss of consortium ₹40,000 and funeral expenses ₹15,000, to be enhanced by 10% every three years.

t: 'Golden hour' as defined in Section 2(12A) of the amended MV Act means:
o: The 48 hours within which the First Accident Report must be filed
The one-hour period within which the police must reach the accident spot
The one-hour period following a traumatic injury during which prompt medical care is most likely to prevent death
The first 24 hours after an accident within which the FIR must be lodged
e: Section 2(12A) defines golden hour as the hour after a traumatic injury with the highest likelihood of preventing death by prompt medical care; s.162 provides for cashless treatment during this period.

t: Under the motor accident claims scheme (Rule 150A / CMV Rules, effective 01.04.2022), the Investigating Officer must submit the First Accident Report (Form I) to the Claims Tribunal within:
o: 90 days of the accident
30 days of the accident
10 days of the accident
48 hours of the accident
e: The FAR (Form I) goes to the Tribunal within 48 hours; Form II (rights of victims) within 10 days; the Interim Accident Report (Form V) within 50 days and the Detailed Accident Report (Form VII) within 90 days.

t: Under the pre-amendment Section 161, hit-and-run compensation for death and grievous hurt was respectively:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The old Solatium Scheme amounts were ₹25,000 (death) and ₹12,500 (grievous hurt); the 2019 amendment raised these to ₹2 lakh and ₹50,000 and dropped the term 'Solatium Fund'.

t: Under Section 157 of the MV Act, on transfer of ownership of a vehicle the certificate of insurance is deemed transferred and the transferee must apply to the insurer for change of particulars within:
o: 30 days
14 days
60 days
7 days
e: Section 157 deems the policy transferred along with the vehicle for third party purposes; the new owner must apply within fourteen days for the necessary changes in the certificate and policy.

t: Under Section 185 of the MV Act, a person is deemed to be driving under the influence of alcohol if the blood alcohol level exceeds:
o: 50 mg per 100 ml of blood
20 mg per 100 ml of blood
30 mg per 100 ml of blood
80 mg per 100 ml of blood
e: Section 185 fixes the limit at 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood detected by a breath analyser (or other prescribed test). Drunken driving is also a specified defence for the insurer under s.150(2).

topic: Third party – who is not a third party
t: A goods carriage carrying cement also carries three labourers who had paid the driver for a lift. On an accident the labourers are injured. Under the amended Section 147 they are:
o: Third parties entitled to compensation from the insurer under the Act policy
Gratuitous passengers of a goods carriage, specifically excluded from statutory third party cover
Covered as owners of goods under Section 147(1)(b)(i)
Covered as co-workers on a transport vehicle under Section 145
e: Section 147 as amended specifically excludes gratuitous passengers of a goods vehicle; only the owner of the goods or his authorised representative travelling in the vehicle is covered.

t: A claimant whose MACT case was settled before a Lok Adalat later wishes to appeal, feeling the amount was low. Legally:
o: An appeal lies to the High Court within 90 days under Section 173
No appeal lies, because a Lok Adalat award is based on consent of the parties and is final
A revision lies to the District Judge within 30 days
The award can be reopened by the Claims Tribunal on an application under Section 166
e: Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 settle disputes by consent; their awards are deemed decrees of a civil court and are not appealable.

t: On receiving a Detailed Accident Report, the designated officer of the insurer makes an offer of settlement which the claimant accepts before the Tribunal. The insurer must pay the amount within:
o: 15 days from the date of acceptance
30 days from receipt of the record of settlement
90 days from the date of the offer
6 months from the date of the accident
e: Under s.149(3)(a) the Tribunal records the consent settlement and payment must be made within a maximum of thirty days from receipt of the record of settlement.

t: Under Section 149, after the insurer receives information of an accident, the designated officer may make an offer of settlement to the claimant before the Claims Tribunal within:
o: 30 days
12 months
90 days
60 days
e: Section 149(2) provides for the designated officer to make an offer within thirty days following the prescribed procedure; if rejected, the Tribunal fixes a hearing on merits.

t: A truck insured under an Act policy is driven by a person whose licence had been suspended for six months and the accident occurs during the suspension. The insurer's position under Section 150(2):
o: The insurer must pay and cannot recover from the owner under any circumstances
Breach of the specified condition regarding a disqualified driver is available as a defence
The defence is available only if the owner was also driving
No defence is available since the driver once held a valid licence
e: Section 150(2)(a)(ii) allows the insurer to defend on the ground of driving by a person not duly licensed or disqualified from holding a licence during the period of disqualification.

t: A cyclist is killed by a vehicle that speeds away; despite police efforts the vehicle is never traced. Six months earlier the same family received ₹50,000 as interim relief from a State fund for this accident. Under Section 161 the family is entitled to:
o: ₹2,00,000 in addition to the ₹50,000
Nothing, since the vehicle is unidentified and no insurer is liable
₹2,00,000 less the ₹50,000 already received, i.e. ₹1,50,000
₹5,00,000 under Section 164 since death resulted
e: A hit-and-run accident is one where the identity of the vehicle cannot be ascertained despite reasonable efforts; compensation is ₹2 lakh for death, and any compensation received earlier for the same accident is adjusted.

t: Under the amended Section 159, the police officer must prepare and submit the accident information report to the Claims Tribunal within:
o: Forty-eight hours
Six months
Thirty days
Three months
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Section 159 requires the police officer, during investigation, to prepare an accident information report in the prescribed form within three months and submit it to the Claims Tribunal and other prescribed agency.

t: The widow of a scooterist killed by a truck files under Section 164 and receives ₹5,00,000. She then files a petition under Section 166 claiming ₹30 lakh on proof of negligence. Position:
o: She may pursue s.166, but the ₹5 lakh paid under s.164 is deducted from any compensation awarded; alternatively, if s.164 payment was accepted as full and final, no further claim lies
The s.166 petition is barred because negligence need not be proved under s.164
She must refund the ₹5 lakh before the s.166 petition can be registered
She is entitled to ₹30 lakh in addition to ₹5 lakh, as the two sections are independent
e: Section 164 payment is fixed and final in nature, and compensation paid under any other law or provision for the same accident is deducted; a claimant cannot receive both sums cumulatively.

t: An accident occurs in District A; the claimant resides in District B and the owner of the offending vehicle resides in District C. The claim petition under Section 166 may be filed before the Claims Tribunal of:
o: District C only, where the defendant resides
District A, B or C – at the claimant's option
District B only, where the claimant resides
District A only, where the accident occurred
e: Section 166(2) allows filing before the Tribunal having jurisdiction where the accident occurred, where the claimant resides or carries on business, or where the defendant resides.

t: The owner of a vehicle fails to contest a claim and the Tribunal suspects collusion between claimant and owner. The Tribunal may:
o: Implead the insurer, who may then contest on all grounds available to the owner
Direct the insurer to pay the amount claimed without inquiry
Transfer the case to the Lok Adalat
Dismiss the claim for want of prosecution
e: Section 170 permits the Tribunal, where it finds collusion or failure to contest, to implead the insurer, which may then contest the claim on all or any of the grounds available to the person against whom the claim is made.

t: A cleaner employed on a goods truck dies when the truck overturns due to the driver's negligence. His dependants may claim compensation:
o: Only under the Employees' Compensation Act, since he was a workman
Under both Acts cumulatively
Only under the MV Act, since the accident involved a motor vehicle
Either under the Employees' Compensation Act, 1923 or under the MV Act, but not under both
e: Section 167 gives the claimant an option where the death or injury gives rise to a claim under the Employees' Compensation Act as well as the MV Act – compensation may be claimed under either but not both.

t: Non-disclosure of a material fact by the proposer makes the contract:
o: Void ab initio
Voidable at the option of the insurer
Illegal
Automatically continued on revised terms
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Breach of utmost good faith renders the contract voidable, not void; the insurer may elect to avoid it (subject to Section 45 for life).

t: Under the detailed accident report scheme, the insurer's response to the Tribunal in Form XI (accepting liability with an offer, or disclosing grounds to contest) is to be filed within:
o: 90 days
60 days
10 days
30 days
e: After the DAR (Form VII) reaches the Tribunal within 90 days, the insurer files Form XI within 30 days either accepting liability with an offer of compensation or stating grounds to contest.

t: A passer-by takes an injured accident victim to hospital. The hospital insists on his personal details and the police want to summon him repeatedly. Under Section 134A:
o: He is deemed a witness to negligence and must be impleaded
He is protected from civil or criminal liability and may give evidence by affidavit or video conferencing at his convenience
He becomes liable for the victim's treatment cost
He must appear personally before the Tribunal in every hearing
e: Section 134A protects Good Samaritans who voluntarily and without expectation of reward help a victim; rules provide for examination at their convenience and evidence through affidavit/video conferencing.

t: A road accident victim is admitted to a designated hospital under the Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025. The maximum cashless treatment entitlement is:
o: ₹2.5 lakh per victim for up to fifteen days
₹5 lakh per victim for up to thirty days
₹50,000 per victim for the golden hour only
₹1.5 lakh per victim for up to seven days from the accident
e: The 2025 Scheme notified under s.162 provides cashless treatment up to ₹1.5 lakh per victim for a maximum of seven days from the date of the accident through designated hospitals.

t: A driver holding an LMV (non-transport) licence drives a goods carriage of GVW 6,800 kg and causes an accident. The insurer repudiates for absence of a transport endorsement. As per Mukund Dewangan (2017) and Rambha Devi (2024):
o: The insurer must pay and recover, since the licence was fake
The driver is validly licensed only if the GVW is below 3,000 kg
The driver is validly licensed; no separate transport endorsement is needed for a transport vehicle of GVW up to 7,500 kg
The driver is unlicensed and the insurer is fully absolved
e: Mukund Dewangan held that an LMV licence holder can drive a transport vehicle with GVW not exceeding 7,500 kg without a separate endorsement; the Constitution Bench in Rambha Devi (2024) affirmed this.

t: A car is sold under an informal agreement and possession handed over, but the RC is not transferred under Section 50. The car later causes a fatal accident. Following Brij Bihari Gupta, liability rests on:
o: The registered owner, and the insurer must indemnify him
Neither party, since the sale was incomplete
The purchaser in possession alone; the insurer is discharged
The RTO for failing to effect transfer
e: Until formal transfer under s.50, the registered owner remains liable for the vehicle's use, and the insurer cannot avoid indemnity merely because possession was informally transferred.

t: A salaried permanent employee aged 32, earning ₹30,000 per month, dies in a road accident in December 2024, leaving a wife and two minor children. Applying Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi (with Magma v. Nanu Ram for consortium and the 10% enhancement of conventional heads per three-year span), the total compensation is:
e: Annual income 3,60,000 + 50% future prospects = 5,40,000; less 1/3 personal expenses (3 dependants) = 3,60,000; × multiplier 16 = 57,60,000. Conventional heads at +20%: consortium 48,000 × 3 = 1,44,000, estate 18,000, funeral 18,000. Total ₹59,40,000.

t: A self-employed shopkeeper aged 52 earning ₹25,000 per month dies in an accident. Dependants: wife, one son and mother. The loss of dependency as per Pranay Sethi is:
e: 3,00,000 + 10% future prospects (self-employed, above 50) = 3,30,000; less 1/3 for 3 dependants = 2,20,000; × multiplier 11 (age 51–55) = ₹24,20,000.

t: A bachelor aged 24, in permanent employment at ₹15,000 per month, dies in an accident in 2025. His parents are the only dependants. Total compensation including conventional heads (at +20%) is:
e: 1,80,000 + 50% = 2,70,000; bachelor with only parents → deduct 1/2 = 1,35,000; × 18 = 24,30,000. Add filial consortium 48,000 × 2 = 96,000, estate 18,000, funeral 18,000 → ₹25,62,000.

t: Non-salaried deceased, age 45, income ₹12,000 per month, dependants mother, wife and two children; petition filed April 2024. Following the standard worked method (future prospects 25%, multiplier 14, deduction 1/4, conventional heads +20%), the total award before interest is:
e: 15,000 × 12 = 1,80,000 × 14 = 25,20,000 less 1/4 = 18,90,000 loss of dependency. Add estate 18,000, consortium 48,000 × 4 (spousal, two parental, one filial) = 1,92,000, funeral 18,000 → ₹21,18,000.

t: On a contested award of ₹21,18,000 the Tribunal grants 7.5% simple interest from the petition date to the date of deposit, a period of 610 days. The interest amount (approx.) is:
e: Interest = 21,18,000 × 7.5% × 610/365 = ₹2,65,475. TDS is then deducted on interest exceeding ₹50,000 per claimant (10% with PAN, 20% without).

t: The interest component of an award is ₹2,65,475 payable to a single claimant who has furnished PAN. The TDS to be deducted and the net interest paid are:
o: TDS nil; net ₹2,65,475
e: Interest above ₹50,000 per person attracts TDS at 10% where PAN is furnished (20% otherwise): 2,65,475 × 10% = 26,547, net ₹2,38,928.

t: A Claims Tribunal awards ₹3,50,000. The insurer wishes to appeal. The minimum amount to be deposited for the appeal to be entertained is:
e: Section 173 requires deposit of ₹25,000 or 50% of the award, whichever is less. 50% of 3,50,000 = 1,75,000, so ₹25,000 is deposited.

t: Deduction for life insurance premium under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act is available up to an overall limit of:
o: ₹1 lakh
₹1.5 lakh
₹2 lakh
₹2.5 lakh
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). ₹1,50,000 aggregate for all 80C items; premium qualifies only up to 10% of the sum assured for policies issued after 1 April 2012.

t: A married deceased leaves behind wife, three children, father and mother (six dependants). The fraction to be deducted towards personal and living expenses is:
e: Pranay Sethi: married with 2–3 dependants deduct 1/3; 4–6 dependants deduct 1/4; more than 6 deduct 1/5. Six dependants → 1/4.

t: For an accident in 2025, the deceased leaves a wife and two children. Total compensation under conventional heads (loss of estate, consortium for all three claimants, funeral) applying the 10% enhancement per three-year span since 2017 is:
e: Two three-year spans since October 2017 give +20%: consortium 48,000 × 3 = 1,44,000, loss of estate 18,000, funeral expenses 18,000 → ₹1,80,000.

t: In a single hit-and-run accident, one pedestrian dies and two others suffer grievous hurt. Total compensation payable from the Hit and Run Compensation Fund under Section 161 is:
e: Death ₹2,00,000 + grievous hurt ₹50,000 × 2 = ₹3,00,000, paid from the Hit and Run Compensation Fund under the Motor Vehicle Accident Fund (s.164B).
